title: How Often Does the Field Flip?
subtitle: Teaching generative models the physics of dynamos, from a compass to the research frontier
title_options: How Often Does the Field Flip?
Exact Where It Is Exact: physics-constrained generative models for dynamos
status: outline v2 (reviews applied; to be validated by the user)
logline: No one can yet say when Earth's magnetic field will flip next, but in the dynamos we can compute, we can learn how often. One film climbs from a compass to the frontier of physics-constrained generative AI for dynamos.
synopsis: It opens on a compass needle that flips and on the striped seafloor, then builds the physics picture by picture: stretch versus smudge, thresholds, and a liquid-sodium experiment, VKS, that flips like the Earth. Chaos hides the date of the next flip, yet a shuffled box of snapshots, plus the equations, still holds the crossing rate, through Rice's formula. Generative models then learn to dream such snapshots between the knob settings that were simulated. At its heart is one lesson from an independent, prospective internship study around the MilaDy project: enforce each law where it is true, exactly for every field, or on average for the crowd. Small CPU experiments show what works and what fails. It ends on written bets for 3D dynamos, VKS and DRESDYN, filled in as simulations arrive.

chapters.title: Cold open: the needle and the stripes
chapters.learning_goal: Feel that Earth's field is not permanent: it has flipped many times, irregularly.
chapters.takeaway: The field has flipped many times, with no schedule; we can ask when, and we can ask how often.

scenes.title: A needle that flips
scenes.key_idea: This needle has pointed north your whole life; the rocks say it has pointed south too, again and again.
scenes.visual: Stylized 3D compass in macro, no hand (G3). The vermillion needle tip swings and settles north; at about 7 s it swings round to south, holds, and settles back north. The polarity needle (M1) is born here; later it appears as a small corner needle only in scenes where the dipole D is on screen (E7).
scenes.on_screen: chip 'illustration, not to time scale'

scenes.title: Pull back to the planet
scenes.key_idea: The needle follows a field that wraps the whole planet. It feels permanent. It is not.
scenes.visual: 'Powers of Ten' zoom made of flat layered illustrations cross-faded on scale (compass, room, landscape), ending on a grey sphere where vermillion dipole field lines bloom from pole to pole. Only the last 3 s are WebGL, rendered as a separate shot (G4). The narration describes what is on screen (A3).
scenes.on_screen: chip SCHEMATIC

scenes.title: The seafloor tape recorder
scenes.key_idea: Cooling lava freezes the field's direction; the spreading seafloor records it as stripes of uneven width: the flips are irregular.
scenes.visual: Cross-section of a mid-ocean ridge: magma rises and cools, short grain segments align with the field and freeze, the floor slides away on two conveyor belts. Stripes accumulate mirror-symmetrically as a true barcode: solid vermillion = normal, near-background = reversed, labels kept (A5). The camera tilts down on the barcode, whose widths are visibly irregular; it slides left and becomes the polarity strip under a thin D(t) trace (T1 morph).
scenes.on_screen: labels 'normal' / 'reversed'; 'every few hundred thousand years, irregularly' (no powers of ten at L0); chip SCHEMATIC; reference chip (to be sourced)
flags: EXTERNAL_FACT: seafloor magnetic stripes (Vine and Matthews 1963), source before use (decision D7)

scenes.title: Two questions
scenes.key_idea: When will it flip next? How often does it flip? In the dynamos we can compute, the first is hopeless and the second is not.
scenes.visual: Two cards: 'When will it flip next?' with a grey clock, 'How often does it flip?' with amber tally marks. The clock card's border turns dashed and dims; the tally card stays lit. On the words 'machines that dream up magnetic fields', a 3-s teaser of the violet cloud (M4), the film's second protagonist (A6).
scenes.on_screen: the two questions; violet-cloud teaser
sources: P4:1627 (when vs how often, shown for the three-mode model)

scenes.title: Title
scenes.key_idea: Title card.
scenes.visual: Title words sit in a vermillion field-line field; the dipole flips and the lines reorganise around the letters; one soft impact sound (SFX event, G2).
scenes.on_screen: working title (decision D13)

chapters.title: A planet that makes its own magnet
chapters.learning_goal: Understand that the field must be regenerated by moving liquid metal, that a dynamo is a self-amplifying loop with a threshold, and that physics prefers neither polarity.
chapters.takeaway: A moving conducting fluid can turn a tiny field into a large one once its loop gain passes a threshold, and the laws do not prefer north or south.

scenes.title: No magnet inside
scenes.key_idea: Left alone, a field in Earth's core would fade within some ten thousand years; the field is billions of years old, so moving liquid iron must keep regenerating it.
scenes.visual: Flat Earth cutaway in grey shells (solid inner core, liquid outer core). A 'left alone' timer makes a field fade in about 10^4 years while a geological clock runs on to billions of years. Then the outer core starts to churn, drawn as a Canvas 2D advected texture (G5: no full-screen shader). Grey matter, no colour until fields appear.
scenes.on_screen: 'liquid iron outer core'; 'a field left alone fades in about 10,000 years' vs 'the field is billions of years old'

scenes.title: Lines never end
scenes.key_idea: Cut a magnet in half and you get two magnets, never a lone north pole: field lines never start or stop, so through any box as many lines enter as leave.
scenes.visual: Surprise first (C5): a bar magnet is sawn in half and each half has both poles. Then iron filings morph into vermillion field lines; a dashed box is dragged around the picture; two counters 'in' and 'out' always agree. Planted for div B = 0 (payoff in 08.2-08.3).
scenes.on_screen: 'lines in = lines out' (no symbol yet)

scenes.title: The squeal
scenes.key_idea: A loop whose gain per turn exceeds one grows from almost nothing, then saturates.
scenes.visual: Opens on a bicycle dynamo: motion makes electricity, with a magnet built in; the Earth must make its own magnet (J). A microphone pointed at its own speaker: whisper, then squeal past a green gain knob (M2); the squeal sits in a narration gap (SFX event, G2). Morph into a self-exciting disc: grey copper disc, coil, current arrows; below the threshold the seed dies, above it the field grows turn after turn, then reaches a plateau (the field brakes the disc). A staircase of bars 'each turn: B x (gain / loss)' smooths into the curve e^(s t) (B8).
scenes.on_screen: Predict Q1 with a 3-s hold; after the reveal: 'each turn: B x (gain / loss)', then 'B grows like e^(s t)', s = growth rate (D1)
flags: EXTERNAL_FACT: self-exciting homopolar disc (Bullard 1955), source before use (decision D7)
scenes.predict: Q1: spin a little faster each time: does the field grow a little each time, or nothing until a certain speed? (Answer: nothing, then exponential growth, then saturation.)

scenes.title: Who pays the bill
scenes.key_idea: A dynamo converts mechanical power into magnetic energy and heat; it creates no energy.
scenes.visual: Loop diagram: motor power -> flow (blue) -> field (vermillion) by induction -> 'the field brakes the flow' -> heat (grey). Forces and losses are named in words only (J).
scenes.on_screen: loop labels in words
sources: en/prep/p3 ch. 5 loop diagram (inline SVG, redraw in palette)

scenes.title: Which way is up?
scenes.key_idea: The equations are unchanged under B -> -B: both polarities are equally lawful; which one you get is history.
scenes.visual: Predict card; then a vertical mirror plane (M10) appears; the Earth's field and its mirror twin side by side; the needle flips.
scenes.on_screen: Predict Q2; then 'B -> -B: same equations'
scenes.predict: Q2: physics does not care whether the field points north or south. Which polarity should Earth prefer? (Answer: neither.)

scenes.title: Checkpoint: the big picture
scenes.key_idea: Recap, then the next question: what kind of motion can do this, and how fast must it be?
scenes.visual: Recap with motifs only (needle, barcode, squeal); the altitude rail (M8, left edge) shows for 3 s and climbs one notch. Ends on the open question, not on an exit ramp (E8).
scenes.on_screen: 'Level 0 -> Level 1'; the open question

chapters.title: Stretch, smudge, and three tanks of sodium
chapters.learning_goal: See a dynamo as a race between stretching and smudging measured by Rm, understand why liquid-sodium dynamos are hard and turbulent, and meet the three that worked, including VKS, which flips.
chapters.takeaway: A flow amplifies a field when stretching beats smudging; only three sodium experiments got there, and one of them, VKS, flips like the Earth.

scenes.title: Frozen threads
scenes.key_idea: A conducting flow drags field lines; stretching a line strengthens the field; diffusion smudges it, faster in a poorer conductor.
scenes.visual: Blue tracer particles stretch and fold a vermillion material line (brightness follows stretch). Split screen with the same flow on both sides: slow-smudging ink (good conductor, small diffusivity: threads stay sharp) vs fast-smudging ink (poor conductor, large diffusivity: a grey blur wins). No viscosity metaphor (B5, J).
scenes.on_screen: 'stretching' / 'diffusion'; split labels 'small diffusivity' / 'large diffusivity'

scenes.title: One number for the race
scenes.key_idea: Rm = UL/eta compares stretching with smudging; the growth rate s crosses zero at a threshold Rm_c.
scenes.visual: Green Rm knob turns; a schematic growth-rate curve s(Rm) rises through zero; the zero crossing is marked as the threshold Rm_c.
scenes.on_screen: Rm = U L / eta (U blue, eta green); s = growth rate; chip SCHEMATIC

scenes.title: The sodium problem
scenes.key_idea: Liquid sodium is as runny as water but smudges fields fast (Pm = nu/eta about 1e-5): reaching Rm of 10 to 50 means stirring so hard that the flow is violently turbulent.
scenes.visual: Two gauges: Rm (green) climbs slowly while Re (blue) races to millions; a turbulent texture fills the background. Level lowered to L1: one ratio, no exponents in the narration.
scenes.on_screen: Pm = nu / eta ~ 1e-5; 'Rm ~ 10-50 needs Re ~ millions'; formula layer: Re ~ 1e6-1e7

scenes.title: Three tanks that worked
scenes.key_idea: Only three liquid-sodium experiments have produced a dynamo, each with a different field, and only one of them flips; DRESDYN is trying with precession.
scenes.visual: Horizontal timeline cards (one moment per card): Riga (helical flow; an oscillating, rotating field), Karlsruhe (52 vortex generators; a steady dipole), Cadarache VKS (150 litres of sodium, motors up to 300 kW; a dipole that can flip); a fourth card, dashed: DRESDYN, under way.
scenes.on_screen: names and one plain line each; 'first dynamo: 1999' for Riga and Karlsruhe (R:139)

scenes.title: VKS: two impellers and an iron surprise
scenes.key_idea: Counter-rotating impellers stir liquid sodium; the dynamo appeared only with soft-iron impellers.
scenes.visual: 3D cutaway of the cylinder (grey matter), two bladed impellers counter-rotating, blue flow cells and recirculation; the impeller material is swapped steel -> soft iron: only then does a vermillion axial dipole grow.
scenes.on_screen: chip SCHEMATIC geometry; 'stainless steel: no dynamo' / 'soft iron: dynamo'

scenes.title: VKS flips too
scenes.key_idea: With impellers at different speeds, the lab dynamo reverses irregularly, like the Earth, every minute or two.
scenes.visual: Qualitative D(t) with reversals (VKS figure, panel b) over the barcode strip; the corner needle (M1) is shown because D is on screen, and flips in sync. This re-hooks the cold open at about 6 min (B2). The measured numbers sit on a separate card, not on the qualitative curve (C6).
scenes.on_screen: 'flips every minute or two, irregularly'; separate card '16 Hz vs 22 Hz: polarities last 120 s and 50 s on average; a reversal takes about 5 s' (Berhanu et al. 2007); curve chip 'qualitative (normal form): durations are not those of VKS'

chapters.title: The equation, the windows, and the question
chapters.learning_goal: Read the induction equation as the race in symbols; know kinematic vs dynamic and the ABC dynamo windows; see that the knob is a panel of knobs, that simulations are too costly to cover it, and what this film asks.
chapters.takeaway: A dynamo can switch on, off and on again, real dynamos depend on many knobs, and simulations cover only a handful of settings: we need something that fills the gaps, and respects the physics.

scenes.title: The induction equation, term by term
scenes.key_idea: The whole race in one equation.
scenes.visual: Equation built with the 10-step protocol: terms light in narrative order, leader lines to a stretched thread ('carried and stretched by the flow', C1) and a fading thread ('diffusion'); pen beats (M9) circle each term.
scenes.on_screen: dB/dt = curl(u x B) + eta Laplacian(B); braces 'carried and stretched by the flow', 'diffusion'

scenes.title: A conveyor belt that does not feel its cargo
scenes.key_idea: Kinematic dynamo: the flow is imposed and the field grows exponentially (an eigenvalue problem). Dynamic: the field pushes back on the flow and saturates.
scenes.visual: Log plot of |B|(t): a straight line of slope s (kinematic), then the same curve bending into a plateau when the field pushes back on the flow (dynamic). One idea only: no Lorentz-force symbol and no anti-dynamo chip here (F2, E6).
scenes.on_screen: 'kinematic: B = e^(s t) B_hat, s = real growth rate (modes may also oscillate)'

scenes.title: Twisting rooms: the ABC flow
scenes.key_idea: To test our tools we need a flow simple enough to write on one line, yet able to make a dynamo: the ABC flow, whose streamlines are corkscrews (velocity parallel to its curl).
scenes.visual: The motivating line first (C3). A periodic box of fat blue corkscrew streamlines (Three.js Line2), slow orbit, long lens. The box glows for a moment on the faint staircase map (M7, tier-2 preview, E1).
scenes.on_screen: u = (A sin z + C cos y, B sin x + A cos z, C sin y + B cos x);  curl u = u

scenes.title: Predict: once on, always on?
scenes.key_idea: Dynamo windows: the ABC dynamo switches on near Rm 9, off near 17.5, on again above about 27.
scenes.visual: Predict card; then s(Rm) drawn live, left to right, from E3 (24 points); windows shaded green at 12%; inset z = 0 slices of |B| of the dominant mode (least damped or fastest growing) at Rm 8, 12, 16 and 20: below, inside and just after the first window (B7). The 48^3 check markers move to X1.3 (F3).
scenes.on_screen: thresholds 'about 9 · 17.5 · 27'; formula layer: 8.87 / 17.6 / 26.8 (32^3) vs published 8.9 / 17.5 / about 27; source chip DATA · E3
flags: CAVEAT: kinematic test bench, no generative model in E3
scenes.predict: Q3: lowering diffusion only helps stretching; once the dynamo turns on, it stays on. Right? (Answer: no, windows.)

scenes.title: A panel of knobs
scenes.key_idea: The control parameter is a vector: Re, Rm, materials, boundary conditions, forcing asymmetry, precession.
scenes.visual: The single green knob splits into a panel (Re, Rm, iron, asymmetry, precession). One boundary-condition switch moves a threshold marker up by about 40%, with the chip 'simulations, Nore et al. 2018' (B15). The three definitions of Rm leave this scene (they live in X6.0).
scenes.on_screen: knob names in words ('iron', not mu_r: D3); 'boundary condition: threshold +40% (simulations)'; formula layer: Rm_c = 90 ± 5 (pseudo-vacuum) -> 130 ± 10 (vacuum) at Re = 1.5e3, mu_r = 50

scenes.title: A handful of dots
scenes.key_idea: Each 3D turbulent simulation is expensive, so only a few knob settings exist, each a huge dataset.
scenes.visual: A green parameter axis with a few filled dots; each dot grows a tall grey stack of data files; the gaps between dots stay empty.
scenes.on_screen: 'each simulation: a few settings, terabytes'; chip 'order-of-magnitude estimate' (C12)

scenes.title: The question of this film
scenes.key_idea: This study asks: can a machine learn the family of possible fields for any knob setting, respect physics exactly where it is exact and statistically where it is statistical, and tell us how often the field flips?
scenes.visual: Lower-third 1, on screen for at least 4 s and not narrated (J): the project context (B1). Then 'This study asks:' and the question, typeset word by word in the colour key, splits into three promise cards that the film ticks off on screen at 05.3, 08.6 and 09.1 (F6); a small violet cloud sits on card 1 (A6). The staircase map of the film (M7) appears with tiers 0-4 all grey (E1). Lower-third 2 with one spoken sentence: the disclaimer (F4; former C3.8 folded in).

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Level 1 done
scenes.key_idea: Full simulations cost too much, so we start with a caricature that has three dials and already flips.
scenes.visual: Motif recap (threads, knob panel, barcode); rail (left edge) shows for 3 s and climbs to L2; ends on the bridge sentence into ch04 (C4, E8).

chapters.title: Chaos and the shoebox of photographs
chapters.learning_goal: See reversals in a three-mode model, understand why 'when' is unpredictable, and why the stationary distribution (a shuffled box of snapshots) is the stable object; meet crowd laws.
chapters.takeaway: The date of the next flip is unknowable, but the cloud of states is stable, and some laws hold only for the cloud.

scenes.title: Three dials
scenes.key_idea: Three coupled modes (quadrupole Q, dipole D, velocity V) with the B -> -B symmetry already reverse.
scenes.visual: Three dials (D vermillion, Q light vermillion, V blue) linked by springs; then the equations appear term by term in the same colours; the staircase map lights tier 0 (E1).
scenes.on_screen: Qdot = 0.119 Q - V D;  Ddot = -0.1 D + V Q;  Vdot = Gamma - V + Q D;  (Q, D, V) -> (-Q, -D, V); coefficients as numbers only (D3); chip 'phenomenological model (Gissinger 2012)'

scenes.title: Two whirlpools and a corridor
scenes.key_idea: Below Gamma about 0.86 each trajectory is trapped in one of two mirror whirlpools; above, a corridor opens and it flips.
scenes.visual: Live RK4 integration in Canvas: (Q, D) phase portrait with a fading trail; green Gamma knob turned from 0.80 to 1.00; the two mirror whirlpools touch; a two-note sound at each crossing (SFX events, G2); scrolling magnetogram strip D(t) with its barcode underneath.
scenes.on_screen: Gamma knob value; chip 'attractor-merging crisis (shown in mu by Gissinger 2012; expected in Gamma)' (C3)

scenes.title: Listen to the rate
scenes.key_idea: We count every time D crosses zero (most crossings are flips, some are near-misses): the crossing rate switches on at a threshold between Gamma = 0.86 and 0.865 and grows with Gamma.
scenes.visual: Ticks per zero crossing; the simulated crossing rate vs Gamma builds point by point (41 values); training values as filled dots.
scenes.on_screen: 'crossing rate: 0 up to 0.86 · about 2 per 1,000 time units at 0.865 · about 11 per 1,000 at 1.00' (F5, D5); formula layer: 0.00194 and 0.0112 per unit time

scenes.title: Predict: when is the next flip?
scenes.key_idea: At Gamma = 0.9, errors grow by a factor e every ~11 time units while the mean interval between crossings is about 230: 'when' is out of reach.
scenes.visual: Predict card; two trajectories started 1e-6 apart at Gamma = 0.9, drawn in two shades; their separation on a log axis climbs with slope ~0.09; a ruler compares 11 units with the ~230-unit mean interval (B12).
scenes.on_screen: 'Gamma = 0.9 · Lyapunov time ~11 · mean interval between crossings ~230'
sources: D fine grid (0.00442 crossings per unit time at 0.9)
scenes.predict: Q4: we know the state to six decimals. Can we predict the date of the next reversal? (Answer: no.)

scenes.title: The long exposure
scenes.key_idea: Above the threshold, different trajectories paint the same glow: the stationary distribution is reproducible. Below it, each start paints one whirlpool.
scenes.visual: At Gamma = 0.93, shown on screen, two trajectories from different starts leave long-exposure glows that converge to the same shape; an amber histogram of D (bimodal) builds below and becomes identical for both. One closing line: below the threshold, each start paints its own whirlpool (B6).
scenes.on_screen: 'Gamma = 0.93'; 'the long-exposure glow (stationary distribution)' (B5: mu_Gamma is kept for X2 and X4)

scenes.title: The shoebox
scenes.key_idea: Cut the film into frames, shuffle, drop the timestamps: a sample of the stationary distribution. A snapshot carries no timestamp and no time order.
scenes.visual: A film strip of the trajectory is cut into frames that fall, shuffled, into a shoebox; their time labels flutter away; the box's contents redraw the same cloud.
scenes.on_screen: 'a snapshot carries no timestamp and no time order' (A4)

scenes.title: Crowd laws
scenes.key_idea: dE/dt fluctuates from snapshot to snapshot; only its mean is zero. The energy budget is a law of the crowd.
scenes.visual: Each shoebox photo drops a marble into an amber histogram of dE/dt (computed from the model's right-hand side); the histogram breathes around zero; its mean marker sits exactly at 0. A bank-account ledger flashes as a preview.
scenes.on_screen: 'true on average, not for each'; amber E[P - eps] = 0 (eps = dissipation, never D: D4)

chapters.title: Counting crossings from still photographs
chapters.learning_goal: Understand Rice's formula as 'a toll counter without a clock' and see it reproduce the true crossing rate from snapshots plus the equations.
chapters.takeaway: A shoebox of snapshots plus the equations gives the crossing rate without running time forward.

scenes.title: A toll counter without a clock
scenes.key_idea: From one aerial photo with readable speedometers, count cars in a thin strip, weight by speed, divide by the width: crossings per hour.
scenes.visual: Aerial highway with a line across it; a thin strip around the line highlighted; cars inside the strip glow with their speed; a counter computes the rate; no clock anywhere.
scenes.on_screen: 'rate = (cars in strip x speed) / strip width'

scenes.title: Rice for the dipole
scenes.key_idea: For D, the strip is |D| < h and each snapshot's speed Ddot = -0.1 D + V Q comes from the equations.
scenes.visual: Shoebox points spread in the (D, Ddot) plane; the strip |D| < h (h = 0.2) lights up; each point's |Ddot| is drawn as a bar; equation morph to the formula with pen beats (M9). Only about 21 of the 8,000 reference points at Gamma = 0.9 fall in the strip: zoom on the strip and use a denser re-integrated set (C13).
scenes.on_screen: r_0 = lim_{h->0} (1/2h) E[ |Ddot| 1{|D|<h} ] (r_0 = crossings per unit time, D3); reference chip 'Kac 1943; Rice 1944-1945'
flags: DATA: for a dense strip, re-integrate one long Gissinger trajectory at Gamma = 0.9 in the extractor (CPU seconds), or read experiences/resultats/cache_e1/sim_fine.pkl (local only)

scenes.title: Check against the truth
scenes.key_idea: On the true distribution, with no time order, Rice reproduces direct counting with a cumulative error of 4% near the threshold and 6% above.
scenes.visual: Rates vs Gamma: direct count (solid vermillion) and Rice on reference snapshots (amber) drawn on together. 'Cumulative error' is defined visually once: the shaded area between the two curves divided by the area under the true curve (C7); the same shading returns in 09.1. Promise card 3 gets a first tick.
scenes.on_screen: 'cumulative error 4% (0.865 <= Gamma <= 0.885) · 6% (Gamma >= 0.89)'; source chip DATA · E1

scenes.title: Crossings are not reversals
scenes.key_idea: Rice counts every zero crossing, near-misses included, not only clear-cut reversals.
scenes.visual: One caveat card: a D(t) trace with an excursion that touches zero and returns is counted. The other caveats move: 'needs the equations' and 'a rate, not waiting times' to 09.1, 'tested on a 3-variable deterministic system' to X4.1 (F).
scenes.on_screen: 'crossings, not reversals'

scenes.title: Photographs on demand
scenes.key_idea: So all we need is a cheap source of snapshots at any knob setting. But how do you get snapshots at a setting nobody simulated?
scenes.visual: The green parameter axis from 03.6 returns, gaps glowing; rail (left edge) shows for 3 s and climbs to L3; ends on the open question (E8).
scenes.on_screen: 'Level 2 -> Level 3'

chapters.title: A machine that dreams snapshots
chapters.learning_goal: Understand conditional flow matching as learning an average wind from noise to data, conditioned on the knob, and how generated distributions are judged against a noise floor with a distribution distance.
chapters.takeaway: A generative model learns a wind that carries noise to data, one model for every knob setting, judged against the noise floor.

scenes.title: From noise to data
scenes.key_idea: A wind field carries a cloud of random points onto the shape of the data.
scenes.visual: Round violet Gaussian cloud (M4); a time-dependent wind bends particle paths onto two symmetric blobs; granular hiss under the motion (SFX event, G2).
scenes.on_screen: 'generative model: new, plausible examples on demand'

scenes.title: Two clocks, two velocities
scenes.key_idea: The generator's time t in [0, 1] is not physical time, and its velocity v_theta (violet) is not the fluid velocity u (blue).
scenes.visual: Side-by-side chips: violet clock 't: transport time' vs grey clock 'physical time'; violet arrow v_theta vs blue arrow u. Moved before the formulas that use t and v (C6).
scenes.on_screen: 'the generator makes snapshots, not movies'

scenes.title: Straight strings, average wind
scenes.key_idea: Training is plain regression: at each place and moment, learn the average direction of straight noise-to-data strings.
scenes.visual: Thousands of straight strings from noise points to data points; at a probe location the passing strings average into one violet arrow; the learned trajectories, drawn with transport time t on the horizontal axis (1D state vs t), curve but never cross (C9); pen beats (M9) on the regression target.
scenes.on_screen: x_t = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1;  J(v) = E || v(x_t, t, lambda) - (x_1 - x_0) ||^2;  v* = E[x_1 - x_0 | x_t, lambda] (lambda = the knob, green)

scenes.title: Turn the knob, reshape the cloud
scenes.key_idea: One model for a continuum of knob settings, including settings never simulated, between those that were (interpolation).
scenes.visual: Green knob drives lambda; target blobs drift and the violet cloud follows; on the knob axis training values are filled dots, test values open dots. Ends with generated violet photos dropping into the 04.6 shoebox (E3).
scenes.on_screen: 'trained on filled dots, tested on open dots (interpolation only)'

scenes.title: The noise floor
scenes.key_idea: Two honest samples of the same truth differ; compare models with that floor at equal sample size, never with zero. A distribution distance measures how far apart two crowds are.
scenes.visual: A die rolled 1000 times, twice: two amber histograms differ; their distance becomes a dashed grey floor line. Then an 8-s 'distance between crowds' beat: the earth-mover picture, sand moved from one histogram onto the other (B6). The formula is not narrated (F).
scenes.on_screen: dashed 'floor'; amber 'distribution distance'; chip 'technical names: energy distance (used in the experiments), Wasserstein W1 (earth-mover)' (D2, B6); formula layer only: E(P, Q) = 2 E||X - Y|| - E||X - X'|| - E||Y - Y'||

chapters.title: The mirror and the crowd
chapters.learning_goal: On the three-mode model: see a plain generator inherit the data's polarity bias, a built-in mirror fix it at every knob value while augmentation fixes it only where data exist, the budget check stay blind to the mirror, and a crowd law forced onto each snapshot become a spike; meet the two-jury estimator.
chapters.takeaway: Build the mirror into the machine, impose crowd laws on the crowd, and never force a crowd law onto each snapshot.

scenes.title: A lopsided machine
scenes.key_idea: A plain conditional model reproduces the cloud's shape but inherits the training data's polarity imbalance.
scenes.visual: Opens on two empty shelves labelled in plain words, 'true for every snapshot' and 'true only for the crowd' (C1: the taxonomy becomes the chapter pair's payoff, 08.6). Then (Q, D) clouds at Gamma = 0.85: reference (grey, chip SIMULATED) vs baseline model A (violet chip GENERATED); a polarity balance bar shows A's tilt. Ends on a question mark at the mirror.
scenes.on_screen: two empty shelves; 'Gamma = 0.85, a value never seen in training'

scenes.title: Predict: the mirror test
scenes.key_idea: A mirror built into the network keeps both polarities equally likely at every knob value. It is built into the machine but acts on the crowd: each snapshot stays lopsided, the crowd is balanced.
scenes.visual: Predict card (one student learns from mirrored copies, the other has a mirror built in); (Q, D) clouds A vs C at 0.85; the mirror gate S acts on the violet cloud: each generated point stays on one side, the crowd balances (C2). The mirror card is placed on the crowd shelf with the tag 'built in, exactly'.
scenes.on_screen: shelf tag 'built in, exactly'; formula layer: v_sym = 1/2 [v(x) + S v(S x)], S = diag(-1, -1, 1)
scenes.predict: Q5: one student learns from mirrored copies, the other has a mirror built in. At an unseen knob value, who stays symmetric? (Answer: the built-in mirror.)

scenes.title: Only where the data are
scenes.key_idea: Augmentation symmetrizes only at the knob values it was trained on; between them the network interpolates freely.
scenes.visual: Training data lopsided below the threshold (P(D > 0) = 0.375 at Gamma 0.80, 0.3125 at 0.86). Asymmetry vs Gamma for A, B, C drawn per Gamma (train filled, test open) against the dashed floor: A spikes, B dips only at training values, C sits on the floor everywhere.
scenes.on_screen: 'A: 0.183 at 0.86, 0.085 at unseen 0.87 · B: 0.003-0.006 at training values, 0.007-0.025 between them (mean 0.016) · C: about 0.004 (floor) everywhere' (B11)

scenes.title: The budget is blind to the mirror
scenes.key_idea: Any mix of the two polarities passes the energy-budget check, so symmetry must be imposed separately.
scenes.visual: A slider p mixes the two whirlpool clouds; the amber budget gauge stays at zero for every p; the lopsided model A even scores best on the budget check (B4).
scenes.on_screen: 'A: lowest budget-check residual of A, B, C (0.0167 vs 0.0223 and 0.0217)' (C7); formula layer: Remark 3.7

scenes.title: Predict: balance every snapshot?
scenes.key_idea: Forcing the stationary budget onto each snapshot makes a spike that the truth never produces: worse where it counts (Corollary 6).
scenes.visual: Predict card; bank-account ledger; the amber dE/dt histogram of 04.7 (reference, Gamma = 0.93) and a hand that pushes every marble onto zero: the histogram collapses into a spike. Numbers land after the picture. The budget card goes on the crowd shelf. Closing line sets up 08.5: 'in the next test, a cruder score is fooled by the same spike' (A10).
scenes.on_screen: 'distribution distance x9 (0.0231 vs 0.00257) · spread of dE/dt -> 4e-17'; formula layer: Cor. 6: no atom at 0 => any law on {L phi = 0} is singular: KL = infinity ('infinitely surprised'), W1 >= E|L phi| / Lip(phi) (B6)
scenes.predict: Q6: energy in must equal energy out. Force every snapshot to balance exactly: better or worse? (Answer: worse.)

scenes.title: Enforce it on the crowd, with two juries
scenes.key_idea: Impose the budget on the generated distribution during training, even at knob values with no data; estimate it with two independent half-batches.
scenes.visual: A batch of violet samples votes; squaring one batch mean secretly adds a variance penalty (a hidden spike-maker); splitting into two juries and multiplying their means removes it; pen beats (M9).
scenes.on_screen: E[gbar^2] = (E g)^2 + Var(g)/n;  E[gbar_a gbar_b] = (E g)^2;  S_lambda(theta) = sum_k (E_q[L phi_k] / s_k)^2

chapters.title: Fields have stricter laws
chapters.was: C7.1-C7.4 + C7.9-C7.10 + new (E2 half of C7)
chapters.learning_goal: Meet the 2D MHD test bench; see that clean training data do not give clean outputs, that exact mechanisms (potentials, projection) beat a penalty, that the crowd-level budget loss beats a control run while tilting and per-sample rescaling fail; sort every law onto its shelf.
chapters.takeaway: Enforce each law at the level where it is true: build per-snapshot laws into every output, impose crowd laws on the crowd.

scenes.title: A flat sheet of plasma
scenes.key_idea: A second test bench with whole fields: forced 2D MHD in a periodic square, with one knob, the magnetic diffusivity eta. A flat world cannot sustain a dynamo on its own: this is a training ground for laws, not a dynamo.
scenes.visual: The chapter card declares a side-step on the rail ('new test bench: from three numbers to whole fields', L4 -> L3). The periodic square tiles itself; blue u and vermillion B maps from the reference samples (32^2, zero-padded in Fourier space to 256^2 for display, G7); the green eta knob with 11 values (6 filled training dots, 5 open test dots). The staircase map lights tier 1 (E1). The anti-dynamo payoff is narrated here (E6, B1 of the pedagogy review).
scenes.on_screen: 'forced 2D MHD · periodic square · knob: eta · 6 training values, 5 test values'; chip 'not a dynamo: a planar flow cannot sustain a field (Zeldovich); here B is kept alive by its own forcing'; chip 'display interpolation (spectral)'

scenes.title: Predict: does clean data make clean outputs?
scenes.key_idea: A model trained only on divergence-free fields still outputs a relative divergence of 0.41; a soft penalty only reaches 0.34 (u) / 0.16 (B).
scenes.visual: Predict card; generated u and B maps (same display interpolation; divergence measured on the native grid) at eta = 0.00951, free model V0 vs reference; a divergence map lights up hot spots; the 'lines in = lines out' box of 01.2 fails its count; penalty bars follow. The divergence card goes on the per-snapshot shelf.
scenes.on_screen: 'free: 0.41', then 'penalty: 0.34 (u) / 0.16 (B)'; chip 'penalty inflates magnetic energy x2.7' (F)
flags: HYPOTHESIS label for 'the penalty is gamed by inflating the swirl part'
scenes.predict: Q7: trained only on perfectly divergence-free fields, are the outputs divergence-free? (Answer: no, 0.41.)

scenes.title: Hill maps and swirl minus slope
scenes.key_idea: Generate potentials (a landscape) and take the curl: zero divergence for free. Or project: remove each wave's component along its own direction.
scenes.visual: A landscape psi with water walking its contour lines (the 01.2 box returns: nothing piles up); then Fourier space: each wave's arrow loses its component along k (projector motif M6). A gauge needle drops to 1e-17.
scenes.on_screen: u = (d_y psi, -d_x psi);  u_k -> (I - k k^T / |k|^2) u_k;  gauges: final projection 5e-17 · potentials 1.7e-17 · projected flow 2e-8 (single precision)
flags: CAVEAT: divergence measured with the same spectral operator (P16)

scenes.title: Why almost is not exactly
scenes.key_idea: To land exactly on the constraint, the ideal wind needs a spring that becomes infinitely stiff at the very end; a network of bounded strength cannot, so a residue always remains.
scenes.visual: NIGHT, no ink change: a ball pulled onto a line by a spring whose stiffness meter shoots up near t = 1; a capped spring (bounded network) leaves a visible gap. No formula in the core cut (B3): Proposition 2 and Remark 3.6 live in X2.2.
scenes.on_screen: 'needs infinite stiffness at the end' / 'bounded network: a gap remains'

scenes.title: Three ways to fix a budget
scenes.key_idea: At unseen eta, the crowd-level loss cuts the distribution distance from 2.52 (control run) to 0.70; tilting collapses the effective sample; per-sample rescaling turns the dissipation into a spike while a spectrum-based score even improves.
scenes.visual: Bar race over three lanes with the dashed floor, one number per lane (F): (1) training loss V5 vs a control run of equal length; (2) exponential tilting with an ESS counter ticking down, 'a poll of 500 that shrank to one person' where the model is worst (B10); (3) per-sample rescaling: the dissipation histogram collapses into the spike of 07.5 while the spectrum-based score improves; only the spread of the dissipation reveals it (A10).
scenes.on_screen: lane 1 '0.70 vs 2.52 (control)'; lane 2 'mean ESS/N 0.29 · one effective sample in 500 at the largest test eta'; lane 3 'spread of eps x 8.6e-4 · spectrum-based distance 2.62 -> 1.1: fooled'; chip 'one seed per variant'; the other numbers go to the description and X3.4
flags: CAVEAT: one seed, interpolation only (P10, P11)

scenes.title: Two shelves
scenes.key_idea: Enforce each law at the level where it is true: per-snapshot laws are built into every output, crowd laws are imposed on the crowd; the mirror is a crowd law that can be built in exactly.
scenes.visual: The two shelves of 07.1, now full: every card placed during ch07-ch08 slides to its final place; in the last 10 s the formal row of the report's classes appears under the shelves (C1). Redrawn taxonomy, no blue for per-sample. Promise card 2 gets its tick.
scenes.on_screen: 'Enforce a constraint where it is true'; formal row (last 10 s): C1 x in ker A · C2 c(x) = 0 · C3 g#mu = mu · C4 E_mu[L phi] = 0

scenes.title: The proposed machine
scenes.key_idea: The framework this study proposes, panel by panel; the experiments tested pieces of it only. Checkpoint L3 -> L4.
scenes.visual: The report's framework figure revealed panels a (latent flow to a symmetric law), b (potential decoder) and d (distributional control) only (E9); the tested pieces light up: potentials in 2D, equivariance in 3 variables, the crowd loss, Rice. Rail (left edge) shows for 3 s and climbs to L4; ends on the open question 'so how well does it answer how often?' (E8).
scenes.on_screen: title 'The proposed machine'; chip 'PROPOSED · not implemented as a whole · E1-E3 tested pieces only' (A6); 'Level 3 -> Level 4'

chapters.title: The honest scoreboard
chapters.learning_goal: See the 'how often' payoff with its error bars, why a smooth generator must lag a steep onset, and what remains weak.
chapters.takeaway: On a toy model the crossing rate is predicted from generated snapshots and the model's equations, without running time forward: roughly right far from the threshold and poorly near it, as expected from a generator that varies smoothly with the knob.

scenes.title: How often, from generated photographs
scenes.key_idea: Rice applied to generated snapshots of model C (seed 0) predicts the crossing rate with 14% cumulative error for Gamma >= 0.89 (up to 65% at a single value) and 42% near the threshold.
scenes.visual: The toll counter of 05.1 returns with violet 'generated cars' (E3). The 04.3 curve returns; Rice on reference (amber) and Rice on generated samples of model C (dashed, violet chip) are drawn on, model F faint; the cumulative error is the shaded area of 05.3 (C7). Two caveat chips moved from 05.4. Promise card 3 gets its tick.

scenes.title: Predict: early, late or on time?
scenes.key_idea: Near the threshold the generator leaks a little below, lags at the threshold and overshoots just above.
scenes.visual: Predict card; zoom on 0.80-0.90: tiny spurious crossings below the threshold, a lag at 0.865, an overshoot at 0.875-0.88 (B17).

scenes.predict: Q8: near the threshold, will the predicted crossing rate switch on early, late or on time? (Answer: a little leakage below, late at the threshold, then an overshoot just above.)

scenes.title: A stiff sheet on a steep ramp
scenes.key_idea: A generator that varies smoothly with the knob cannot follow a law whose bridge mass and crossing rate are born with a steep slope (Proposition 9, attenuated form).
scenes.visual: A stiff sheet laid on a steep ramp rounds its knee (no cliff: the symmetrized law varies continuously, A5); then the generated (Q, D) cloud is swept across the 21 Gamma values next to the reference, with the bridge mass P(|D| < 0.25) as a bar that leaks a little below, lags at the threshold and overshoots just above (B17); pen beat on the bound (M9).
scenes.on_screen: chip 'consistent with Prop. 9 · one model, seed 0'; formula layer: W1(q_lambda, q_lambda') <= K |lambda - lambda'|  =>  max error near lambda_c >= (J_delta - 2 K delta) / 2

scenes.title: The loss is not a clean win
scenes.key_idea: On a good model the crowd loss halves stationarity residuals but narrows dE/dt; on a biased model it fails.

scenes.title: Still far from the data
scenes.key_idea: The models remain well above the data's own noise floor; few seeds; interpolation only.
scenes.visual: Spectral error bars of all variants against the data floor on a log axis; seed counters; 'interpolation' chip.
scenes.on_screen: 'spectral error 0.07-0.23 (log10) vs 0.002-0.011 for data · E1: 2 seeds · E2: 1 seed · interpolation only'

scenes.title: Scoreboard and three lessons

chapters.title: The climb to 3D: bets on the staircase

modules.title: The proofs behind the pictures
modules.learning_goal: State Propositions 1-5 and their scope, as the specialists will want them.

scenes.title: Proposition 1: build it in
scenes.key_idea: If the decoder's image lies in the constraint subspace, every sample satisfies the constraint, whatever the training quality.
scenes.visual: PAPER; statement typed on; a decoder box whose output arrows all land on a plane.
scenes.on_screen: Prop. 1 statement

scenes.title: Proposition 2 in full
scenes.key_idea: The optimal flow on a subspace splits into a learnable part and a stiff contraction; a bounded network leaves O(1) residuals.
scenes.visual: PAPER; the formula grows term by term; the contraction term 1/(1 - t) is plotted against t (the spring of 08.4); V3's 2e-8 explained by single precision. Sole home of the formula since 08.4 became intuitive (B3, I5).
scenes.on_screen: v* = m(P x, t) - (I - P) x / (1 - t); Remark 3.6

scenes.title: Proposition 3: the Jensen gap
scenes.key_idea: A penalty on the end-of-path prediction is unbiased for linear constraints and biased for nonlinear ones.
scenes.visual: A curved constraint arc; the mean of two points falls off the arc: the gap is shaded.
scenes.on_screen: Prop. 3 statement

scenes.title: Proposition 4: the mirror, proved
scenes.key_idea: Equivariant velocity + invariant noise give an exactly invariant distribution at every parameter; if each mu_lambda is symmetric, symmetrization never increases the population loss; it doubles network evaluations.
scenes.visual: Mirror gate on the violet flow, then the proof in three lines.
scenes.on_screen: v(g x, t, lambda) = g v(x, t, lambda), g#gamma = gamma => g#q(.|lambda) = q(.|lambda) for every lambda; condition 'if each mu_lambda is G-invariant' on the loss statement (C10); 'cost: 0.5 s vs 0.25 s per 1000 samples'
flags: P22: classical for equivariant flows

scenes.title: Proposition 5 and its limits
scenes.key_idea: For every test function, E_mu[L phi] = 0; the energy budget is one case. Necessary, not sufficient: fixed points and unstable orbits satisfy it too.
scenes.visual: Amber identity, then a fixed point and an unstable orbit each pass the same test (warning lamp); degree <= 2 monomials enforced, degree 3 kept as a control. The generator L and the degrees are introduced here, not in the core (B4).
scenes.on_screen: E_mu[L phi] = 0; Remark 3.11; 'enforced: degree <= 2 · control: degree 3'

modules.title: Crowd laws, deeper

scenes.title: The distribution distance, defined
scenes.key_idea: The energy distance compares two crowds through average pairwise distances; it is zero only when the crowds have the same law.
scenes.visual: The formula built term by term over two point clouds with faint pairwise lines (moved from 06.5, F).
scenes.on_screen: E(P, Q) = 2 E||X - Y|| - E||X - X'|| - E||Y - Y'||; 'called distribution distance in the film' (D2)

scenes.title: The least-distorting correction
scenes.key_idea: Exponential tilting is the I-projection: the reweighting that fixes a mean with minimal KL change, without moving any sample.
scenes.visual: Dots whose size is their weight; the tilted density slides to the target mean; Pythagorean triangle for KL.
scenes.on_screen: q* = e^(beta . g) q / Z(beta);  beta* = argmin log Z(beta) - beta . c (Csiszar 1975); supp q* = supp q (q* for the tilted law, D3)

scenes.title: The poll that shrank

scenes.title: Where the model never went

opening.tts_text: [calm, natural narrator voice] This needle has pointed north your whole life. Rocks on the ocean floor say it has pointed south too. Again and again, with no schedule. [long pause] That needle follows a field that wraps the whole planet. It feels permanent. It is not. Along the ridges of the ocean floor, fresh lava cools, and tiny magnetic grains freeze in place, each remembering which way a compass pointed. As the seafloor spreads, they line up into stripes of very uneven widths. [long pause] So, two questions. When will it flip next? And how often does it flip? In the dynamos we can compute, the first question turns out to be hopeless. The second one is not. Finding out why takes us from this needle to liquid metal, to chaos, and to machines that dream up magnetic fields, and must learn where physics is exact, and where it only holds on average.
opening.notes: The reversal lands at about 7 s and the two questions at about 0:34 (A1). Per-scene word budgets now match the cue map at about 135 words per minute (A2): about 25 / 16 / 36 / 68 words for 11 / 7 / 16 / 30 s. The seafloor sentences rely on an external fact (decision D7). Site-only alternative for 00.3: 'In a tank of liquid sodium in Cadarache, the field flips too.'

closing.tts_text: [calm, natural narrator voice] Back to the compass in your hand. [long pause] We still cannot tell you when this needle will turn around. In the dynamos we can compute, chaos erases the memory of the present too fast. But those dynamos do answer another question: how often. That answer hides in a cloud of snapshots, and a machine can learn to draw such clouds, even between the settings that were simulated. [long pause] On small test problems, it partly works. The mirror symmetry holds by construction. On a three-variable model, the rate at which the dipole crosses zero comes out roughly right far from the tipping point, and poorly right at it, because a smooth machine cannot follow a steep change. The real tests, in three dimensions and in liquid metal, are still ahead. You have seen the bets. [long pause] One lesson remains. Enforce each law where it is true. Exactly, where it is exact. On average, where it only holds on average.
